quiz_support: A function can accept a changing number of positional arguments. In a definition, *scores collects those arguments into a tuple named scores.
A tuple keeps values in order. The star in this parameter position means collect arguments; it is not multiplication.

```python
def show_items(*items):
    print(items)

show_items("map", "lamp")
show_items()
```
The first tuple contains map and lamp; the second tuple is empty.
You can loop over the collected tuple just like another sequence. For a running total, begin at zero and add each supplied number.
In a call, the star has a related unpacking job: show_items(*["map", "lamp"]) passes two arguments. Without that star, show_items(["map", "lamp"]) receives one argument: the whole list.
An empty tuple contributes no additions, so a total initialized to zero remains zero. Return the calculated total rather than printing it.

quiz_support: A bare * in a function definition marks following named parameters as keyword-only. Callers must spell the option name instead of supplying its value by position.

```python
def caption(text, *, loud=False):
    return text.upper() if loud else text

print(caption("Hello", loud=True))
```
This returns HELLO. caption("Hello", True) is rejected because loud must be named. upper returns uppercase text.
**extras in a definition collects additional keyword arguments into a dictionary. It is different from *items, which collects positional arguments into a tuple.
For example, a call with prefix="Note: " stores that value under the key "prefix" in extras. extras.get("prefix", "") reads it or returns the supplied empty-text default when absent.
Accepting arbitrary extra names can hide spelling mistakes. In this exercise, loop over extras and raise ValueError if a key is not "prefix". The loop reads dictionary keys.
The task uppercases only title, not prefix. Choose the transformed title, then join prefix and that title with +. Do not add an extra separator: any desired space belongs to prefix.
Keyword-only arguments clarify call sites. They do not automatically validate the kinds of values, so this exercise states its accepted types.
The supplied __check_error helper is test infrastructure: it reports whether a sample call raises the expected error. Leave it unchanged; your task is make_label.

quiz_support: Optional chaining uses ?. to stop a property lookup when the value immediately before it is null or undefined.
Each possibly missing boundary needs its own protection. user?.profile?.name handles a missing user and a missing profile.
The ?? operator supplies a fallback only for null or undefined. It keeps an empty string; || would replace that empty string too.
Combine the guarded lookup with the fallback for this exercise. An existing name is returned without changing the object.
Optional chaining does not catch every error. It does not make an undeclared variable safe or suppress an exception thrown inside another operation.

quiz_support: A trigger is database work that runs automatically when its specified event happens. Unlike a SELECT, it can cause additional writes.
The supplied database has notes(id,title) and note_audit(note_id,old_title,new_title). Titles are never NULL in this fixture.
In an UPDATE trigger, OLD refers to the row before the update and NEW refers to the row after it. OLD.title and NEW.title read those two title values.

```sql
CREATE TRIGGER log_label
AFTER UPDATE OF label ON demo
WHEN NEW.label <> OLD.label
BEGIN
  INSERT INTO demo_log(old_label,new_label) VALUES(OLD.label,NEW.label);
END;
```
This syntax example assumes demo and demo_log tables exist. It is not a separate setup to paste into the notes exercise.
AFTER means the row update happens before this trigger’s work. UPDATE OF title identifies updates assigning that column, even when the assigned value equals the old value.
WHEN NEW.title <> OLD.title limits the trigger to changed titles. The <> operator means not equal. Use NEW.id for the note identity.
The supplied operations change note1 from Moon to Moon draft, leave note2 at Sea, then change note1 to Moon final. The audit should contain exactly the two actual changes, in their recorded order.
Use the isolated practice data only. Triggers run inside database operations and their effects participate in transactions; test them before applying them to real stored data.

quiz_support: An ETag is a response validator identifying a version of a representation. It is not necessarily a timestamp.
A client can send its saved tag in If-None-Match to ask whether that representation changed.
For a matching GET validator, a server can respond 304 Not Modified without sending the representation body again. The client can reuse its stored representation.
When the tag differs, a normal 200 response sends the representation and its current tag. A changed version must not be described as unchanged.

This browser helper models one exact strong-tag comparison. For example, the text '"v2"' includes quotation marks as part of the HTTP tag. Real HTTP validator parsing has additional rules outside this small exercise.
body:null in this helper means send no response body for304. It is not an instruction to send the JSON text null over HTTP.
This practice uses explicitly public content. Validators do not replace access controls or establish that personalized data is safe to share.

quiz_support: Uncommitted tracked-file edits belong to the working tree. A stash can temporarily save those edits while you work on something else.

Use only a new empty disposable folder, with Git installed and configured. Create note.txt containing first. Then run git init, git add note.txt, and git commit -m "First note" in that folder. Change note.txt to draft and save without committing. Never run this practice inside an existing personal repository.

```bash
git status
git diff
git stash push -m "practice draft"
git stash list
git stash show -p stash@{0}
```
The tracked file returns to its committed content, while the stash keeps the saved difference. Inspect before relying on that result.

```bash
git stash apply stash@{0}
git diff
git stash list
```
apply restores the saved edits but keeps the stash entry. Confirm the file contains draft again and the entry remains listed.
pop tries to apply and, on success, remove the entry. Keeping apply and inspection separate is safer for this exercise; do not drop the stash until the recovered work is verified.
By default, ordinary stash push does not include untracked files. A new untracked file is not protected merely because tracked changes were stashed.
Applying onto conflicting edits can require conflict resolution. A stash is local working-change storage, not a remote backup or a published commit.

explanation: A module is a file with its own scope: names declared inside it do not automatically become available in other files. A top-level import or export makes these example TypeScript files modules.

Put export before a declaration to make it available to other modules. A named import uses braces to select an exported name. The quoted path tells the compiler which file to look for; ./ means the current folder.
An object can match an imported type without creating that type as a runtime value. You can annotate badge with Badge, but you cannot call Badge() or print Badge as if the type itself were a value.
The example prints Badge: Reader. Renaming the local badge variable would not change which function is imported; changing an export name requires changing its corresponding named import.
This is a concept lesson: the embedded editor does not run multiple TypeScript modules. The two complete files above are an optional local companion, not an in-app coding check.

To try the companion locally, use a folder with Node.js and TypeScript installed. Save the two code blocks as badges.ts and main.ts. In that folder run npx tsc --strict --skipLibCheck --target ES2022 --module commonjs --outDir dist badges.ts main.ts, then node dist/main.js. Use a folder without a package.json declaring type: module: this example deliberately emits CommonJS, a Node-compatible module format. Other runtimes may require different module settings or file extensions.
React.lazy(load) declares a component whose loader runs when React first tries to render it. Declare the lazy component outside App so normal App renders reuse the same declaration.
The loader returns a Promise: an object representing a result that may arrive later. A pending Promise has no result yet. Resolving it supplies a result; rejecting it supplies an error.

For lazy, the resolved result must be an object whose default property contains a component. For example, React.lazy(() => Promise.resolve({ default: Greeting })) makes Greeting the loaded component. Promise.resolve creates an already-resolved Promise, so that small example need not visibly wait.

A Suspense boundary surrounds children that can suspend while waiting. Its fallback is the replacement UI shown while the lazy child is pending. Once the child is ready, React renders it instead of the fallback. ```react Preparing greeting

}> ```

React caches the loader Promise and its resolved component for that lazy declaration. Hiding and showing it again does not reload the component code. This does not preserve the child's local state after unmounting, and it is not a general data cache.

If loading rejects, the nearest Error Boundary handles the error; Suspense is for waiting, not a replacement for error handling. Ordinary fetching inside useEffect does not automatically activate Suspense.

This exercise controls a Promise manually so you can inspect waiting without relying on network timing. new Promise(resolve => { ... }) immediately provides a resolve function; finishLoading saves a callback that resolves it with { default: Report }. The Report code is already present: this simulates a pending module and does not split or download a real file.
